newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WTO chief looks to IT tariff accord at trade meet.
newsitem.headline: WTO chief looks to IT tariff accord at trade meet.

text.p: World Trade Organisation chief Renato Ruggiero said on Tuesday he hoped to see a global accord on scrapping tariffs on information technology products (ITA) at next week's WTO Ministerial Conference in Singapore.

In an interview with Reuters, he said he was also looking for the ministers from the WTO's 125 member states to give a push to completion of a world-wide pact on opening up telecommunications markets by next February's deadline.

And he expressed optimism that next year a solution would be found to allow China -- which will be in Singapore as an observer a long 10 years after it began talks on joining -- -- entry to the world trade body.

"An IT agreement and one on telecommunications would would be essential elements in the liberalisation of the new technologies which will be at the heart of progress in the next century," the WTO Director-General declared.
"These two are in my mind essential for trading into the future," he added.

The United States has set an IT accord which would remove all duties on computer hard- and software, semi-conductors and telecommunications equipment by the year 2000 as its own top priority for the Ministerial, from December 9-13.
Analysts say an agreement on these lines would open up trade worth over $400 billion a year.

Washington is strongly backed in the issue by Japan and Canada. The European Union supports a deal but is not in full tune with the other three top trading powers on the timing and products it would cover.

At last week's summit meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (APEC), the United States also won reluctant backing from Asian countries, many of them exporters of IT products -- boosting hopes of a deal in Singapore.

An earlier bid in the WTO to negotiate an accord on basic telecommunications, which would allow foreign firms into national markets, failed in April when the United States pulled out arguing developing countries were holding back.
But the talks have resumed, given fresh life by new U.S. and EU market opening offers, and negotiators say they aim to complete them by February 15.

Ruggiero said he believed the main impetus IN THIS AREA likely to emerge from Singapore would come from meetings behind the scenes there during the Ministerial -- the two-year-old WTO's first -- of senior technical experts on telecoms.

The WTO chief and former Italian trade minister told Reuters he did not foresee a major confrontation at the gathering between developed and developing countries over "new issues" of trade and labour, investment and competition policy, or on textiles and agriculture.
Disagreements on how these topics should be handled in the declaration to be issued by the ministers at the end of the meeting prevented WTO ambassadors from finalising a text in Geneva last week.
"Every good trade negotiation must have a moment of suspense and some moment in which everybody believes there is a dramatic confrontation," the 66-year-old Ruggiero said.

"We had a good negotiation on the declaration and at the end we have left some problems to the ministers, which are certainly very sensitive from a political point of view. But the substantial differences, I would say, are really marginal."
He said China -- like the ITA and telecomms -- was part of the "less visible" agenda at Singapore which was "perhaps the most important part" of what would be discussed there.

"Now is the time to solve the still existing, and still difficult, problems that China's entry to the organisation creates. But I think that in 1997 it is possible we could find the right solution," the WTO chief declared.
